author: GamingBolt
description:
MARVEL Tōkon: Fighting Souls reads like the perfect package: intuitive mechanics, awestriking visuals, and a pumping soundtrack, all wrapped up in Marvel tag-team flavour. Few fighting games away from the ‘Big Three’ generate the immediate excitement Tōkon: Fighting Souls has, but chuck in developer Arc System Works’ pedigree and the 4v4 brawler has the potential to be an all-timer. 

See, ArcSys is responsible for some of the best-received anime-infused fighting games of the last decade, with the studio now looking to deliver a genuine evolution of the fast-paced, three-on-three tag-fighter formula that the genre has sorely lacked in recent years. If MARVEL Tōkon: Fighting Souls sticks the landing, it could become one of 2026’s biggest games, but this won’t be down to hype and reputation alone.
title: Why MARVEL Tōkon Fighting Souls Could Be One of 2026’s Biggest Games

author: GamingBolt
description:
Fittingly, then, Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game’s greatest achievement isn’t simply about making each victory feel satisfying. It’s that improvement itself is rewarding. 

Make no mistake, extensive combos are easy to drop, but the game rarely discourages you. Perhaps through its suite of awestriking basic manoeuvres, the approachability of its combo extensions, or simply the sensory impact of a pair of fighters zooming across an arena, the game consistently communicates why you should keep playing. 

What initially seemed contradictory, or even intimidating, soon becomes an act of expression, and one you’ll be happy to engage with long after you’ve mastered the auto combo into launch.
title: Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game Review - The Final Verdict

author: GamingBolt
description:
When you hear descriptions about superficial complexity in gaming, the most common one to come up is, “Wide as an ocean, deep as a puddle.” But what about the inverse? What does “deep as an ocean, wide as a puddle” look like? Call me crazy, but I think that's Marathon in a nutshell.

It's something I called out in my review, way back when. Those who sought a hardcore extraction shooter experience with exceptional polish and excellent gunplay would be best served. As punishing as matches could feel due to the UESC bots and the smaller map size, which made it easier for players to collide; as non-social as playing solo felt, instead likened to a survival horror experience (especially if you're Rook); and as awful as the menus felt, it occupied a niche between ARC Raiders and Escape From Tarkov. 

It felt as focused and confident with its gameplay as its setting did with all the moths and fonts. There was depth to build on – new directions that it could go in.
title: As Player Numbers Drop, Can Marathon's New PvE Mode Save It?
